transcript:
[doctor] Hello there! How are you doing today?
[patient] Hi, Doctor. I’ve been better, honestly. I’ve been having a lot of pain.
[doctor] Oh, I’m sorry to hear that. Can you tell me more about the pain you’re experiencing?
[patient] Sure. It’s been this really bad epigastric pain right here in the upper middle part of my stomach. It’s been going on for about three weeks now.
[doctor] I see. How would you describe the pain? Is it sharp, dull, burning?
[patient] It’s pretty intense, especially after I eat. It feels like a burning pain.
[doctor] Hmm, that sounds quite uncomfortable. Are there any other symptoms you’ve noticed?
[patient] Yes, I’ve been feeling nauseous a lot, and sometimes I even throw up. I also feel really bloated.
[doctor] I see. Has this pain affected your daily activities or sleep?
[patient] Yes, it has. It’s been really hard to eat, and my sleep is all messed up because of the pain.
[doctor] I’m sorry you’re going through this. Have you noticed anything that makes the pain better or worse?
[patient] Eating definitely makes it worse. Sometimes, not eating at all helps a bit, but then I just feel weak and tired.
[doctor] That’s tough. Have you tried any over-the-counter medications or home remedies to relieve the pain?
[patient] I’ve tried some antacids, but they don’t seem to help much.
[doctor] Okay, thank you for sharing all that. Can I take a look at your medical history?
[patient] Yes, here you are.
[doctor] Based on your medical history, I see you had a peptic ulcer a few years ago. Is that correct?
[patient] Yes, that’s right. It was a few years ago, but I haven’t had any issues since then.
[doctor] Understood. Let’s go through a quick review of your symptoms. Besides the epigastric pain, nausea, and bloating, are you experiencing any shortness of breath or cough?
[patient] No, I haven’t had any shortness of breath or cough.
[doctor] How about chest pain or palpitations?
[patient] No chest pain or palpitations either.
[doctor] Good to know. Let’s check your vital signs. Your blood pressure is 130/80 mmHg, heart rate is 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute, and your temperature is 98.6°F. Everything looks normal there.
[patient] That’s good to hear.
[doctor] Now, let’s do a physical exam. I’ll start with your abdomen. Please lie down for me.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] I’m palpating your epigastric area now. Do you feel any tenderness here?
[patient] Yes, that’s where it hurts.
[doctor] I see. But no rebound tenderness or guarding, which is good. Let me check your heart sounds.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] Your heart sounds are normal, and I don’t hear any murmurs. Now, let’s listen to your lungs. Take a deep breath in and out for me.
[patient] (Deep breath)
[doctor] Your lungs are clear on both sides. Lastly, let’s do a quick neurological check. Follow my finger with your eyes.
[patient] (Follows finger)
[doctor] Everything looks good neurologically. Based on your symptoms and exam, it seems like your epigastric pain might be due to acid reflux or a recurrence of peptic ulcer disease.
[patient] Oh no, that doesn’t sound good.
[doctor] Don’t worry; we can manage this. I’ll prescribe you Omeprazole 20 mg once daily for four weeks. This should help reduce the acid in your stomach and relieve your pain.
[patient] Okay, I can do that.
[doctor] In addition to the medication, I recommend some lifestyle changes. Avoid spicy and acidic foods as they can aggravate your condition.
[patient] I’ll try my best to avoid those.
[doctor] It’s also important to quit smoking if you smoke. Smoking can worsen acid reflux and delay healing.
[patient] I do smoke sometimes. I’ll try to quit.
[doctor] That’s great to hear. Regular exercise and moderate physical activity can also help improve your overall health.
[patient] I’ll try to be more active.
[doctor] Excellent. We’ll re-evaluate your symptoms in four weeks to see how you’re doing with the treatment. If your symptoms persist, we might need to do an upper GI endoscopy to get a better look at what’s going on.
[patient] Okay, I understand.
[doctor] In the meantime, I’ll give you some educational materials on GERD and peptic ulcer management. It’s important to understand your condition and how to manage it effectively.
[patient] Thank you, Doctor.
[doctor] You’re welcome. If your symptoms worsen or if you develop any new symptoms, please don’t hesitate to come back to the clinic sooner.
[patient] I will. Thank you for your help.
[doctor] Take care, and I’ll see you in four weeks.
[patient] Alright, see you then.
